Feel
fēl
v. (to perceive by touch; to grope; to experience; rendering Hebrew mashash, yada, and bin, Greek pselaphao)
Old English fēlan, to touch, perceive. In the Authorized Version the word is nearly always the hand's work — Isaac feeling Jacob, Samson feeling for the pillars, the Athenians feeling after God.

Biblical Definition

Paul at Athens: God made the nations “that they should seek the Lord, if haply they might feel after him, and find him, though he be not far from every one of us” (Act 17:27). Isaac: “Come near, I pray thee, that I may feel thee, my son, whether thou be my very son Esau or not” (Gen 27:21), after Jacob had feared, “My father peradventure will feel me, and I shall seem to him as a deceiver” (Gen 27:12). Egypt's ninth plague was “darkness over the land of Egypt, even darkness which may be felt” (Exo 10:21). Samson asked to “feel the pillars whereupon the house standeth” (Jdg 16:26). “Whoso keepeth the commandment shall feel no evil thing” (Ecc 8:5). “Before your pots can feel the thorns, he shall take them away as with a whirlwind” (Psa 58:9).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines feel as to perceive by the touch; to have sensation excited by contact; to try by touch; to be affected by; to experience.

expand to see more

FEEL, v.t. To perceive by the touch; to have sensation excited by contact of a thing with the body or limbs.

2. To have the sense of; to suffer or enjoy; as, to feel pain; to feel pleasure.

3. To try; to sound; to search; as, to feel after a thing in the dark.

4. To perceive; to know.

Key Scripture

Act 17:27 — "That they should seek the Lord, if haply they might feel after him, and find him, though he be not far from every one of us:"

Gen 27:21 — "And Isaac said unto Jacob, Come near, I pray thee, that I may feel thee, my son, whether thou be my very son Esau or not."

Gen 27:12 — "My father peradventure will feel me, and I shall seem to him as a deceiver; and I shall bring a curse upon me, and not a blessing."

Exo 10:21 — "And the LORD said unto Moses, Stretch out thine hand toward heaven, that there may be darkness over the land of Egypt, even darkness which may be felt."

Ecc 8:5 — "Whoso keepeth the commandment shall feel no evil thing: and a wise man's heart discerneth both time and judgment."

Psa 58:9 — "Before your pots can feel the thorns, he shall take them away as with a whirlwind, both living, and in his wrath."

Modern Corruption

Feeling is made the organ of faith, and the one man in Genesis who trusted his hands over his ears blessed the wrong son.

expand to see more

Isaac's blindness made him rely on touch, and touch deceived him. “The voice is Jacob's voice, but the hands are the hands of Esau” — he had the truth in his ears and overruled it with his fingers, and the blessing went by the goatskin. The modern Christian who tests his standing by what he feels is Isaac at the tent door. Faith cometh by hearing, and the assurance that comes by feeling is exactly as reliable as the hair on Jacob's hands: it was real hair, it was really felt, and it was on the wrong man. The word of God is the voice; the feelings are the gloves.

Acts 17:27 is Paul's diagnosis of natural religion. The nations were set in their times and bounds that they might feel after God — the Greek is the groping of a blind man — and Paul's next clause is the point: though he be not far from every one of us. Men grope for a God who is at their elbow, because the groping is done in the dark of Exodus 10, a darkness that may be felt. Natural theology can reach out; it cannot see. Athens had altars to an unknown God because feeling after Him is the most that feeling can do, and the apostle's sermon ended, as it had to, with a man God raised from the dead.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew mashash (H4959), to feel, grope; yada (H3045), to know, experience; bin (H995), to perceive; Greek pselaphao (G5584), to handle, grope after.

expand to see more

Hebrew mashash (H4959) — to feel, grope; Genesis 27:12, 27:21–22, Exodus 10:21, Judges 16:26, Deuteronomy 28:29.

Hebrew yada (H3045) — to know, experience; Ecclesiastes 8:5; bin (H995), Psalm 58:9.

Greek pselaphao (G5584) — to touch, grope, feel after; Acts 17:27, Luke 24:39, 1 John 1:1, Hebrews 12:18.

Usage

"“That I may feel thee, my son” — the hands overruled the voice, and blessed the wrong son."

"“If haply they might feel after him… though he be not far from every one of us” — groping at His elbow."

"“Darkness which may be felt” — the ninth plague."
